title: Eviction threshold and burst policy postmortem
body:
Summary:

On 2025-03-10 we observed increased tail latency and token loss for customers on the eu-west dedicated GPU pools. The immediate user impact was degraded throughput for a small set of high-concurrency tenants (approx 6% of active Dedicated clients) between 03:12 and 08:46 UTC. The root cause was an interaction between an aggressive node eviction threshold (GPU memory reclaim policy) and the recent burst autoscaling policy changes that removed a minimum stabilization window. Together these caused repeated node evictions and rapid scale-down/scale-up cycles (autoscaler thrash), producing backpressure at the scheduler and long queueing for in-flight KV cache warmups.

Why this is different from previous incidents:
- Not a single noisy process saturating GPU compute, but a noisy allocation pattern: a small set of tenants issuing many short-lived, high-concurrency sessions that kept KV caches warm and prevented effective bin-packing.
- Autoscaler configuration allowed immediate scale-down on low utilization which amplified transient memory pressure reactions from the eviction controller.
- Existing eviction metrics focused on utilization per-device, not on per-tenant cache pressure or total warm-KV count, so we reacted to symptoms rather than the underlying cache retention behavior.

Detection and impact:
- First alert: prom-alert "dedicated_gpu_pool_avg_token_latency_p95 > 1200ms" triggered at 03:18 UTC. Pager notified eng-sre primary.
- Customer-reported tickets increased from baseline 2/hr to 14/hr during incident window (customers mostly on Dedicated eu-west-2).
- Measured effects:
  - p95 token latency rose from 250ms to 1.35s
  - GPU memory reclaim events increased by 420% vs 24-hour baseline
  - Autoscaler events: 11 scale-downs and 9 scale-ups between 03:30-05:10 UTC for the affected pool
  - CPU scheduler queue depth increased 3x for the serving runtime pods

Timeline (abridged):
- 03:12 UTC: first elevated latencies observed by Canary.
- 03:18 UTC: prom alert fired and page routed to SRE oncall (Maya).
- 03:25 UTC: initial hypothesis (noisy neighbor) — evict offending pod groups. Executed soft-evict for 3 pods.
- 03:32 UTC: eviction controller reclaimed memory, scheduler rescheduled several tenants onto the same nodes, KV cache warmups increased request tail latency.
- 03:40 UTC: autoscaler observed reduced utilization and triggered scale-down (2 nodes).
- 03:48 UTC: metric oscillation observed; autoscaler brought nodes back up at 03:52 UTC.
- 04:10 UTC: realized oscillation pattern; disabled immediate scale-down (reapplied temporary stabilization window via emergency override).
- 04:22 UTC: mitigation: increased eviction_threshold from 0.82 -> 0.9 for affected pool, and temporarily enforced per-tenant concurrency cap of 150 concurrent sessions.
- 05:10 UTC: latency trending back toward baseline, customer tickets slowed.
- 08:46 UTC: full stabilization and incident declared resolved after 6-hour observation.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- Emergency autoscaler override: set scaleDownStabilizationSeconds=600 for eu-west dedicated pool to prevent rapid scale-down.
- Raised eviction threshold to allow more headroom for KV caches on nodes while we investigated (0.82 -> 0.90).
- Applied per-tenant soft concurrency caps on the 4 most aggressive tenants (150 concurrent sessions), which prevented new short-lived sessions from thrashing caches.
- Increased replica scheduling spread: temporary anti-colocation rule to avoid packing the same tenants' replicas onto the same hosts (rebalanced over 30 minutes).

Root cause analysis (contributing factors):
1) Eviction policy tuning too aggressive: the eviction controller used a single-device utilization model and was not aware of warm-KV count or per-tenant working set sizes. With many short-lived sessions, memory appeared "spiky" triggering evictions even though aggregate useful cache (warm KV) existed.
2) Autoscaler configuration removed scale-down stabilization in recent release (PR ref in linked_artifacts). That meant nodes could be removed quickly in response to short dips, which increased scheduling churn.
3) Lack of telemetry: we had no direct metric for "warm_kv_count" or "per-tenant-kv_pressure" exposed to Prometheus/alerting; existing dashboards only showed device-level memory and overall GPU utilization.
4) Scheduler packing heuristics favored CPU/throughput density over KV affinity. This caused multiple hot tenants to be colocated when the scheduler rescheduled after evictions, increasing pressure.

Why the applied mitigations fixed the symptoms:
- Longer scale-down stabilization prevents nodes being removed during transient dips, reducing churn.
- Higher eviction threshold reduced aggressive reclaiming of GPU memory and gave KV caches time to be reused rather than being torn down.
- Per-tenant concurrency caps reduced the creation rate of short-lived sessions and prevented rebuild storms of KV caches.

Post-incident action items (owners and due dates):
- SRE-101: Instrument per-tenant KV pressure metrics and export to Prometheus (owner: Diego Alvarez) — due 2025-04-04.
- SRE-102: Update eviction controller to consider long-lived KV usage as weighted "pinned" memory (owner: Priya Singh) — RFC by 2025-04-11.
- SRE-103: Revert autoscaler to include a default scaleDownStabilizationSeconds=300 in the configuration and add configurable policy per pool (owner: Maya Chen) — rollout by 2025-04-01.
- SRE-104: Scheduler affinity tweak: add "kv-affinity" hint so replicas of the same tenant prefer different physical hosts (owner: Liam O'Connor) — proposal 2025-03-28.
- SRE-105: Run chaos tests (scale/evict interplay) on a staging dedicated pool to validate new settings (owner: eng-sre) — test plan by 2025-04-15.
- SRE-106: Customer communication: postmortem write-up & outreach to affected accounts (owner: Customer Success - Priya) — by 2025-03-22.

Runbook draft additions (to add to eviction/runbook playbook):
- Add a check: if autoscaler executed >3 scale-downs in 20m and eviction events >5 in 20m then set "troubleshoot-mode" and disable scale-down for 15-60m with oncall acknowledgement.
- Add a play: when p95 token latency > 800ms and eviction events spike, temporarily increase eviction threshold by +0.05 and monitor for 20m.
- Add metrics to surface in the runbook top banner: warm_kv_count (per pool), eviction_events_per_minute, autoscale_event_rate, per-tenant_concurrency_95th.
- Add a step-by-step noisy-tenant isolation checklist: identify top tenants by warm_kv_count -> apply soft concurrency cap -> throttle token_rate -> request tenant engineering outreach.

Longer-term proposals (engineering work):
- Augment eviction controller to maintain a map of "pinned" ranges that represent warm-KV lanes. Eviction should prefer evicting non-pinned allocations. (SRE-102)
- Autoscaler policy engine: implement hysteresis and a minimum up-time for nodes that can be tuned per-pool. Add simulated load policy to evaluate decisions in dry-run mode.
- Enhancements to scheduler: treat KV affinity like disk locality; prefer spreading tenants with high warm_kv_count.
- Tenant-level QoS: introduce soft and hard QoS classes with enforcement in scheduler and runtime.

Open questions / discussion points:
- What is the right default eviction_threshold across all Dedicated pools? 0.9 seems safer but increases overall capacity needs and costs. Do we prefer a slightly higher baseline or pool-specific tuning?
- How quickly can we instrument warm_kv_count in runtime without adding prohibitive metrics overhead?
- Should burst/autoscale policies differ by customer tier (enterprise vs self-serve)?

Runbook: oncall quick checklist (concise):
1) Acknowledge pager and confirm affected pool(s).
2) Check dashboards: p95 token latency, eviction_events, autoscale_event_rate, warm_kv_count (if available).
3) If autoscaler thrash detected (>3 scale-downs in 30m): enable emergency stabilization (scaleDownStabilizationSeconds=300-600).
4) If eviction_events spike: bump eviction_threshold by 0.03-0.08 for the pool and observe 20m.
5) Identify top 5 tenants by warm_kv_count; apply soft concurrency caps and inform solutions/SE.
6) If p95 remains > 1s after 60m, escalate to platform-eng and consider temporary routing to an alternative pool/region.

Customer impact & comms notes:
- Affected accounts were contacted proactively; CS lead prepared personalized notes highlighting mitigations and timelines. (See SRE-106).
- We offered credits to accounts that experienced >5% request error rate during incident window.

Retrospective conclusions:
- Primary failure mode was not compute saturation alone but a systemic interaction between memory eviction and fast autoscaler scale-down.
- The platform must be aware of cache semantics (warm_kv) when making eviction and scheduling decisions.
- Conservative stabilization knobs in autoscaling are valuable even at the cost of some transient underutilization.

Appendix (commands run during mitigation):
- kubectl patch hpa dedicated-eu-west -p '{"spec": {"behavior": {"scaleDown": {"stabilizationWindowSeconds": 600}}}}'
- runtime-ctl set-pool-eviction-threshold eu-west 0.90 --reason "emergency: reduce thrash"
- runtime-ctl set-tenant-capacity --tenant-ids t-204,t-321,t-489 --concurrency 150 --temporary true --duration 4h

Notes to reviewers:
- Reviewers: please validate proposed SRE tickets and ownership. Feedback on default eviction_threshold tradeoffs and whether pool-specific policies are warranted is especially welcome.
- This doc is intended as a working postmortem + runbook draft; expect iteration and follow-ups in the next 2 weeks.

-- Maya
